subtitle: Study the history, languages, faiths and naming practices of Eritrean Minnesotans, how Eritrean and Ethiopian communities differ and what ties they share, and how to plan respectful DHS service.
audience: For all DHS and DSD employees, including case managers, eligibility, data, policy and communications staff, who serve Eritrean individuals and families or work with East African community partners.

lessons.title: Independence, national service and the road to Minnesota
objectives: Summarize the main events in Eritrea's modern history, including the independence struggle and border war.
Explain how indefinite national service and restrictions on freedom have driven people to leave.
Describe common routes Eritreans have taken before resettlement.
Identify limits of Minnesota arrival data for Eritreans.
lessons.teaching:
Eritrea sits on the Red Sea in the Horn of Africa. Italy made it a colony in the late eighteen-hundreds, and Britain administered it during and after the Second World War. In the early nineteen-fifties it was joined to Ethiopia in a federation, and over the next decade Ethiopia steadily reduced Eritrea's self-government and then annexed it. A war for independence followed and lasted about thirty years. Eritrea became independent in 1993 after a referendum in which nearly every voter chose independence.

Peace did not last. From 1998 to 2000 a border dispute with Ethiopia became a full war that killed tens of thousands of soldiers. Since then, the government has kept the country on a war footing. Human Rights Watch reported in 2024 that national service is compulsory for men and women from eighteen to forty, officially limited to eighteen months, but often indefinite since the border war. Its report describes punishment of relatives of people who evade service, postponed elections and recognition of only four religious bodies. As a result, Eritreans, many of them young, have left in large numbers.

The routes out are long and dangerous. The Migration Policy Institute describes Eritreans crossing into Ethiopia and Sudan, where many lived for years in camps or cities, and some moving on through Libya and across the Mediterranean, or through Egypt and toward Israel and the Middle East. Trafficking, detention and extortion along these routes are well documented. Recent wars in Sudan and in northern Ethiopia have made those first countries of refuge less safe.

The Minnesota Department of Health reported 117 primary arrivals from Eritrea in 2024. Primary arrivals are people initially resettled in Minnesota, not everyone who lives here or a count of the whole community. People also arrive through other routes or move here from other states. The Eritrean Community Center of Minnesota in St. Paul connects Eritrean Americans to services and culture.
lessons.keyPoint: Eritrea’s independence struggle, border war and reported indefinite national service help explain some migration histories. Arrival data do not describe every Eritrean Minnesotan or any individual’s experience.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Daniel, a DSD policy analyst, is drafting background for an engagement plan on day services. He finds a line in an old planning document that describes Eritreans as a subgroup of the Ethiopian community and proposes to reach them only through an Ethiopian community organization. His colleague Selam says she is not sure that is accurate. The plan is due for review next week, and Daniel wants it to be right.
lessons.question: What should Daniel do?
choices: Keep the description, since Eritrea was once part of Ethiopia and the communities are closely related.
Remove Eritreans from the plan to avoid getting it wrong.

Correct the description to recognize distinct national communities and shared ties. Contact Eritrean-led organizations, check their current capacity, and invite their input without assuming any one group represents everyone.
feedback: Eritrea has been an independent country for decades, and its people fought a long war for that independence. Describing Eritreans as Ethiopian can be deeply offensive and will miss many families.
Leaving a community out of engagement is not a safe choice. It removes their voice from the decision.
This is the strongest choice. It corrects the description and makes room for direct input while recognizing that no single organization speaks for every person.
lessons.reflection: Where might older documents in your area describe a community in outdated or inaccurate ways? How would you know?
lessons.action: Review one engagement list or outreach plan you use. Check whether Eritrean and Ethiopian communities, and other East African communities, are listed separately with their own partner organizations. Suggest corrections to the owner.

check.question: Which statement best explains why many Eritreans have left their country in recent decades?
check.correct: Compulsory national service that has often been indefinite, along with restrictions on political and religious freedom.
wrong: A national program that encouraged young people to study abroad.
A natural disaster that made the country uninhabitable.
check.feedback: Human rights organizations describe open-ended national service, repression, and religious restrictions as the main drivers. Knowing this helps staff understand why some people are cautious about government processes, without assuming any individual's story.

lessons.title: Peoples, languages and ties with Ethiopia
objectives: Identify Eritrea's nine recognized ethnic groups and major languages.
Distinguish Eritrean from Ethiopian identity while describing shared language, script and culture.
Explain why a Tigrinya interpreter may be from Eritrea or Ethiopia and why that can matter.
Plan interpreter requests that ask about language and comfort.
lessons.teaching:
Eritrea recognizes nine ethnic groups: Tigrinya, Tigre, Saho, Afar, Bilen, Kunama, Nara, Hidareb (often called Beni Amer) and Rashaida. Tigrinya speakers are the largest group. Tigrinya, Tigre, Arabic and other languages are spoken; language and ethnic identity do not have a simple one-to-one relationship. Arabic is widely used, especially among Muslim Eritreans and people from the lowlands. Many Eritreans also learned some Amharic, English or Italian through history, schooling or years spent in other countries.

Eritrea and Ethiopia share deep ties. Tigrinya is spoken in both Eritrea and the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia, and some languages in both countries use the Ge'ez script. Orthodox Christianity, food such as injera, coffee ceremonies, and family relationships cross the border. Many families have relatives in both countries. At the same time, Eritrea's national identity was forged through a long war with Ethiopia and a later border war. For many Eritreans, being described as Ethiopian is not a small mistake. Some Tigrinya speakers from Ethiopia, meanwhile, identify strongly as Tigrayan, and recent conflict in northern Ethiopia has added new pain and tension.

These facts matter for language access. A Tigrinya interpreter may be Eritrean or Ethiopian. Qualified interpreters have professional responsibilities. Some people will worry about confidentiality in a small community, or about an interpreter's background or political ties. Do not assume someone's preference from their nationality. Ask neutrally: Is this interpreter a good fit for you? Would you prefer a different interpreter next time? Also confirm the language itself. Ask each person which language they prefer.

When authorized forms or data group Eritrea and Ethiopia incorrectly, raise the issue with the responsible program or data owner. Collect only information needed for an authorized purpose. Grouping Eritreans under Ethiopian or East African can hide the community and its needs.
lessons.keyPoint: Eritreans and Ethiopians share language, script and culture in many ways, but they are distinct national communities. Ask about language and interpreter comfort instead of assuming.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Aster, an Eritrean mother, meets with Kevin, a county disability services worker, about her daughter's services. The Tigrinya interpreter introduces himself and mentions that he grew up in Mekelle, a city in Ethiopia. Aster becomes quiet and gives short answers. After the meeting, she asks Kevin in simple English whether she could have a different interpreter next time, but says she does not want to cause trouble.
lessons.question: What should Kevin do?
choices: Tell Aster the interpreter is certified and neutral, so she should continue with him.
Thank Aster and use the language-access process to request a different qualified interpreter. Record only the preference needed for that process.
Ask Aster to explain what her concern is about the interpreter's background.
feedback: The interpreter may be fully professional, but effective communication depends on the person being able to speak freely. Dismissing her request puts her comfort second.

This is the strongest choice. Follow the language-access process, protect the information recorded, and do not require Aster to disclose personal history. Availability and timing depend on the process.
Pressing for an explanation can put her in an uncomfortable position and may touch on political or personal history she does not want to discuss. The preference itself is enough.
lessons.reflection: How does your team respond when someone asks for a different interpreter? Does the process make it easy or awkward for them?
lessons.action: Ask your language access lead how to request a different qualified interpreter and record only the preference needed under the applicable process.

check.question: Why might a person from Eritrea and a Tigrinya interpreter from Ethiopia speak the same language but still raise a question of fit?
check.correct: Tigrinya is spoken in both Eritrea and Ethiopia, and history, conflict and small-community confidentiality can shape how comfortable a person feels.
wrong: Because Tigrinya in Ethiopia is a completely unrelated language.
Because interpreters from Ethiopia are not allowed to interpret for Eritreans.
check.feedback: The language is shared, and a qualified interpreter from either country can do excellent work. Fit is about the person's comfort and trust, which is why staff should ask rather than assume, and honor requests for a different interpreter.

lessons.title: Faith, family and naming
objectives: Identify the four religious bodies officially permitted in Eritrea and the faith diversity among Eritreans.
Explain how religious restrictions may shape some people's experience.
Describe one common naming pattern and why staff should confirm the names in a person’s records.
Plan scheduling that respects fasting and holy days when asked.
lessons.teaching:
Eritreans are religiously diverse. Human Rights Watch reported in 2024 that the Eritrean government recognized four religious bodies: the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the Roman Catholic Church, the Evangelical Lutheran Church, and Sunni Islam. Christians and Muslims each make up a large share of the population. Other groups, including Pentecostal and other evangelical Christians and Jehovah's Witnesses, have faced arrest and detention, and even leaders of recognized churches have been imprisoned. For some Eritrean Minnesotans, faith is one of the reasons they left. In Minnesota, Eritreans may belong to Orthodox, Catholic, Lutheran, Pentecostal or other churches or to mosques, some of them shared with Ethiopian or other East African communities, and some people are not religious.

Faith can shape daily routines. Orthodox Christians in the region often fast on Wednesdays and Fridays and during longer fasting periods, especially before Easter, avoiding meat, eggs and dairy. Muslim Eritreans may fast during Ramadan and pray at set times. Practice varies widely from person to person. If a meeting involves food or falls on a major holy day, it is fine to ask about preferences, and it is kind to be flexible when someone mentions a fast or observance.

Naming follows a pattern shared with many Ethiopians. One common pattern uses a personal given name followed by a parent's given name, sometimes with a grandparent's name. Naming practices and documents vary; Eritrea's 2015 civil code also provides family-name options. Household members may have different names, and forms may place a name in a family-name field. Staff who expect a shared family surname may think records are mismatched, or may address people incorrectly.

Families are often closely connected across countries. Many people support relatives in Eritrea, in refugee camps, or in other countries. Ask how a person wants to be addressed, which names appear on their documents, and who they want involved. Involvement does not by itself authorize disclosure or decision-making; follow the applicable consent and authority rules.
lessons.keyPoint: Eritreans have diverse faiths and naming practices. Confirm each person’s preferred name and documents, and ask about individual needs rather than making assumptions.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Yonas, a DHS eligibility worker, is reviewing a household case. The mother is listed as Helen Tesfay, the father as Berhane Kidane, and the two children as Luwam Berhane and Robel Berhane. A colleague on the quality team flags the case because the mother's last name does not match anyone else's and asks Yonas to confirm she is part of the household. Yonas wants to handle this respectfully.
lessons.question: What should Yonas do?
choices: Explain to the colleague that the naming pattern is common for Eritrean families, and confirm household composition using the program's standard verification, not the names.
Ask the mother to change the children's last names to match hers to simplify the file.
Remove the mother from the household until she can explain the name difference.
feedback: This is the strongest choice. Different names do not establish household relationships. Follow the program's applicable verification process without requiring a family to share a surname.
Names are part of a person's identity and legal documents. Asking a family to change them to fit a form is inappropriate and could create new document mismatches.
Removing the mother based on a naming pattern could wrongly cut benefits and treats a normal cultural practice as suspicious.
lessons.reflection: What assumptions about family names are built into the checks and forms in your work?
lessons.action: Explain that patronymic naming is one possible pattern, while names and documents vary. Use the program’s standard verification process and ask the person how their name appears in their records.

check.question: In an Eritrean family following the traditional naming pattern, what would you expect a child's second name to be?
wrong: A family surname shared by all relatives.
check.feedback: In this naming pattern, a child’s second name is the father’s given name. Practices and documents vary, so confirm the names a person uses.

lessons.title: Service barriers and respectful practice
objectives: Identify service barriers that may affect Eritrean Minnesotans.
Explain why some Eritreans may be cautious about sharing information with government agencies.
Distinguish needed information from unnecessary questions about status, politics or flight.
Plan a clear explanation of how DHS protects personal data.
lessons.teaching:
Many Eritrean Minnesotans are well established, with long work histories, businesses, churches and community organizations. Others arrived more recently after years in camps or cities in Ethiopia, Sudan or elsewhere. Barriers vary. Some people have limited formal schooling because national service interrupted their education. Some had schooling and professions that are not recognized here. Recent arrivals may be adjusting to housing, work and the benefits system all at once, while also sending money to relatives abroad.

Caution toward government processes is understandable. A 2025 Migration Policy Institute account describes a two percent diaspora tax and requests for letters of apology in connection with consular documents. This reporting does not establish any individual’s experience. Eritreans abroad hold a wide range of views about their government, and diaspora politics can be tense. Some people may worry about who will see their information or whether it could reach officials or community members with ties to them. They may be reluctant to discuss where they have lived, how they left, or who their family is.

For DHS staff, the answer is clarity and restraint. Explain why you are asking for information and who will see it. Use the approved program notice to explain the purpose and intended use, whether the person must provide the information, known consequences of providing or refusing it, and who is authorized to receive it. Ask the data practices contact if the notice or a question is unclear. Collect immigration information only for an authorized program purpose, following applicable rules and notices. Avoid unnecessary questions about political views, national service or travel. If information is required for an authorized process, follow that process and its applicable notice. Many people experienced detention, trafficking or loss along the way, and asking them to retell it can cause harm. If someone shares on their own, listen, acknowledge it, and bring the focus back to what they need.

Good questions help: Which language would you like us to use? Would you like the same interpreter next time, or a different one? How would you like your name written? Who would you like involved? Offer Eritrean-led organizations such as the Eritrean Community Center of Minnesota as an option, and refer status questions to immigration legal services.
lessons.keyPoint: Explain the applicable data practices notice, collect information for authorized purposes, and avoid unnecessary questions about personal history.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Freweini, a woman in her twenties who arrived recently after several years in Ethiopia, is applying for services with help from Mark, a county worker. When Mark asks for her previous addresses, she hesitates and asks who will see the information. Mark's form also has an optional comment box where a previous worker had recorded a client's reasons for leaving Eritrea. Mark is unsure what to say.
lessons.question: What should Mark do?
choices: Tell her all government information is confidential and move on quickly.

Use the approved program notice to explain the purpose, whether the information is required, consequences of providing or refusing it, and authorized recipients. Leave the optional box unused if the history is unnecessary; follow records rules for any existing entry.
Skip the address question entirely so she feels comfortable, even though the program requires it.
feedback: A blanket promise of confidentiality may be inaccurate and does not answer her real question. People deserve a clear and truthful explanation.
This is the strongest choice. Use the applicable notice and avoid collecting unnecessary history. Follow records rules for any existing entry; do not erase it simply because it is sensitive.
Skipping a required question could delay or derail her application. Comfort comes from honest explanation, not from leaving out required steps.
lessons.reflection: How confident are you in explaining who can see the information you collect? Where would you check if you were not sure?
lessons.action: Find the data practices notice (often called a Tennessen warning) that applies to one form you use. Practice explaining it in two or three plain-language sentences, and ask your data practices contact if anything is unclear.

check.question: Why might some Eritrean Minnesotans be cautious about giving personal information to a government agency?
check.correct: Experiences with a repressive government and reported pressure on the diaspora can make people worry about who will see their information.
wrong: Because Eritrean culture forbids sharing any personal information.
Because Eritreans are not eligible for any state programs.
check.feedback: Caution often comes from real experience, not culture alone. Staff can respond by explaining the purpose of each question, who can see the answers, and by collecting only what the service requires.

cards.back: Compulsory service for men and women aged eighteen to forty, officially eighteen months but often indefinite according to human rights reports. A major reason many Eritreans have left.
Human Rights Watch reported in 2024 that four religious bodies were recognized: Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo, Roman Catholic, Evangelical Lutheran and Sunni Islam. Other groups faced persecution.
The language of Eritrea's largest ethnic group, also spoken in the Tigray region of Ethiopia and written in the Ge'ez script.
One common pattern uses a personal name followed by a parent’s given name. Practices and documents vary; confirm the person’s name.
Eritreans and Ethiopians share language, script and culture in many ways, but they are separate national communities. Let people name their own identity.

aid.heading: Language and interpreters
items: Ask for preferred language: Tigrinya, Tigre, Arabic or another.
Ask whether the interpreter is a good fit and use the language-access process for a request for someone different.
Record only the interpreter preference needed under the applicable process.
Do not use children to interpret.

aid.heading: Names, identity and records
items: Recognize that naming patterns vary; confirm the names on the person’s documents.
Do not infer household composition from whether names match; follow standard verification.
Raise inaccurate country categories with the responsible form or data owner.
Let people identify themselves where the information is needed for an authorized purpose.

aid.heading: Trust and data
items: Use the approved notice to explain purpose, whether a response is required, known consequences, and authorized recipients.
Collect immigration information only for an authorized program purpose, following applicable rules and notices.
Avoid unnecessary questions about politics, national service or travel; follow authorized requirements and notices.
Refer status questions to immigration legal services and offer Eritrean-led community organizations as an option.

sources.title: Minority Rights Group — Eritrea country profile
sources.note: Supports Eritrea's colonial history, federation with Ethiopia, independence referendum (99.8 percent), the border war, and its ethnic groups. Percentages are estimates.

sources.title: Human Rights Watch — World Report 2024: Eritrea
sources.note: Supports compulsory national service for ages 18 to 40 that has often been indefinite since the border war, and the four recognized denominations. Advocacy organization's reporting.

sources.title: Migration Policy Institute — Severe Repression in Eritrea Has Prompted Decades of Exodus
sources.note: Supports migration routes through Ethiopia, Sudan, Libya and the Mediterranean, religious restrictions, the diaspora 2 percent tax and letters of apology.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Health — Minnesota Refugee Health Report 2024
sources.note: Supports 117 primary arrivals from Eritrea in 2024. Primary arrivals only; excludes people who moved to Minnesota from other states.

sources.note: Historical primary-arrival series; not a census of the community.

sources.title: GiveMN — Eritrean Community Center of Minnesota
sources.note: Supports the center's stated mission of connecting Eritrean Americans in Minnesota to social services and to their culture. Organization's self-description. Minnesota’s data practices guidance describes notice elements: https://mn.gov/admin/data-practices/data/warnings/tennessen/.
